existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Noiriel’s socio-history connects archival reconstruction to relationships of power and social interdependence.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2012 opening describes a collective project influenced by sociology, not a claim of sole foundation or institutional membership.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Noiriel examines how public language and state classification construct immigration as a social and political problem.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2007 interview opening explicitly treats immigration as construction and representation within labour/social history; not denial of actual migration.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Noiriel explicitly acknowledges Bourdieu’s sociology as an influence on the collective development of socio-history while declining school allegiance.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: First 2012 answer. The collective is described by Noiriel as including his own generation and practice; no formal master–disciple relation or adoption of all Bourdieu’s positions is asserted.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Bourdieu’s later public interventions for presenting political judgments with the undifferentiated authority of researched scholarship.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Second 2012 answer on fundamental research and essays, explicitly naming Raisons d’Agir interventions. This is Noiriel’s critique of the distinction between expertise and public intervention, not a rejection of all Bourdieu’s sociology.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Noiriel explicitly uses Wittgenstein’s game and language-game metaphor to explain socio-history as shared rules of practice rather than an all-purpose theory.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: First 2012 answer, paragraph beginning “La socio-histoire, ce n’est pas une théorie.” A named methodological metaphor, not blanket adoption of Wittgenstein’s philosophy.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Charle identifies methodological proximity to Noiriel’s sociohistory despite their different labels.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own December 2007 email answer, published 2008, 162, rejects an unproductive terminology dispute while appreciating Noiriel’s and Michel Offerlé’s work and the work in their collection. Offerlé and the collective publication programme retain credit; no shared organization, identical interpretation or personal influence is inferred from this limited comparison. The books and collection were not freshly read.
